title: Merge two sorted arrays in-place.
shortTitle: Merge Two Sorted Arrays In-Place — Fill From the Back

s1_definition.profdef: Merging two sorted arrays in-place takes a first array that has extra capacity at its end and a second sorted array, and merges the second into the first so the combined result is sorted, without allocating a separate output array. The technique writes from the back: three pointers start at the last real element of each input and the very end of the first array, and the larger of the two compared elements is placed at the write position, moving backward. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps Rajesh's transactions in a ledger sized with spare blank rows at the bottom, and Priya's smaller sorted ledger must be merged in so the whole thing stays in date order, without opening a brand-new ledger book. Instead of inserting from the top and shoving everyone down, the clerk fills from the bottom-most blank row upward, each time copying down whichever of the two next-largest dates is bigger, so nothing ever gets overwritten before it is placed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Merge from the back, placing the larger of the two tails into the last empty slot, moving backward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merging two sorted arrays in-place takes a first array that has extra capacity at its end and a second sorted array, and merges the second into the first so the combined result is sorted, without allocating a separate output array. The technique writes from the back: three pointers start at the last real element of each input and the very end of the first array, and the larger of the two compared elements is placed at the write position, moving backward. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps Rajesh's transactions in a ledger sized with spare blank rows at the bottom, and Priya's smaller sorted ledger must be merged in so the whole thing stays in date order, without opening a brand-new ledger book. Instead of inserting from the top and shoving everyone down, the clerk fills from the bottom-most blank row upward, each time copying down whichever of the two next-largest dates is bigger, so nothing ever gets overwritten before it is placed.

**One line to remember:** Merge from the back, placing the larger of the two tails into the last empty slot, moving backward.

sections.s2_technical:
The obvious approach merges from the front into a new array and copies back, which uses extra space. To merge in-place into the first array, which has spare capacity at the end sized to hold both arrays, the trick is to write from the back, not the front. Writing from the front would overwrite elements of the first array that have not yet been merged. Writing from the back is safe because the back of the first array is exactly the free space, so you never clobber a value you still need.

You keep three indices. The first, call it i, starts at the index of the last real element of the first array. The second, call it j, starts at the last element of the second array. The third, call it k, starts at the very last slot of the first array, which is the final write position. At each step you compare the element at i with the element at j and copy the larger one to position k, then move that source pointer and k backward by one. You repeat until the second array is fully consumed.

The reason you stop when the second array is exhausted, not when both are, is subtle and important. If the first array's elements are all exhausted first, the remaining elements of the second array still need to be copied into the front of the first array. But if the second array is exhausted first, the remaining elements of the first array are already in their correct positions, because they were never moved, so no further work is needed. Handling this asymmetry correctly is what separates a correct implementation from a buggy one.

A senior point is the write-from-back invariant. At every moment the write pointer k is always at or ahead of the read pointer i, so you can never overwrite an unread element of the first array. This invariant holds because the total number of elements still to place equals the distance from the start to k plus one, which always covers both unread tails. Stating this invariant in an interview demonstrates you understand why the direction matters rather than just memorizing it.

Another senior point is money and stability. For transaction records sorted by date I compare with BigDecimal or a date comparator, and placing the larger first from the back produces a stable, correctly ordered merge. I guard the case where the second array is empty, in which case the first array is already complete.

A small finance-domain example: `int i=m-1,j=n-1,k=m+n-1; while(j>=0){ if(i>=0 && a[i].compareTo(b[j])>0) a[k--]=a[i--]; else a[k--]=b[j--]; }` merges Priya's ledger into Rajesh's spare rows exactly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores Rajesh's monthly transaction amounts in a ledger array that was pre-sized with spare blank slots at the end, and Priya's smaller sorted set of shared transactions must be merged into the same ledger so the combined list stays sorted, without allocating a second ledger. The merge runs on large ledgers so it must be linear and in-place. Merging two sorted arrays in-place is exactly this.

This is exactly how in-place merge works in Java — writing from the back so the spare capacity absorbs values without overwriting unmerged elements.

Problem 2 — Sometimes Priya's set is empty, so the ledger is already complete and nothing should change, and amounts are exact BigDecimal. This shows the empty-second-array edge case and money precision.

What the code will do: a `LedgerMerger` with `mergeInPlace(BigDecimal[] first, int m, BigDecimal[] second, int n)` using the three-pointer back-to-front technique. The demo merges Priya's amounts into Rajesh's pre-sized ledger.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's ledger holds `1000, 2000, 3000` with three spare slots, and Priya's set is `2500, 2600, 5000`.

Step 1: i points at `3000` (index two), j points at `5000` (index two of second), k points at the last slot (index five). We compare `3000` and `5000`; `5000` is larger, so it goes into slot five. Now j moves to `2600` and k moves to slot four.

Step 2: compare `3000` and `2600`; `3000` is larger, so it goes into slot four. Now i moves to `2000` and k moves to slot three.

Step 3: compare `2000` and `2600`; `2600` is larger, so it goes into slot three. Now j moves to `2500` and k moves to slot two.

Step 4: compare `2000` and `2500`; `2500` is larger, so it goes into slot two. Now j moves below zero, so the second array is now fully consumed and the loop ends.

Step 5: the remaining first-array elements `1000` and `2000` are already in slots zero and one in correct order and were never moved, so no more work is needed. The ledger now reads `1000, 2000, 2500, 2600, 3000, 5000`, fully sorted, with no extra array allocated.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T19:10:00Z INFO Merged ledger = [1000, 2000, 2500, 2600, 3000, 5000]
2026-10-26T19:10:00Z INFO Final sorted ledger ready for statement generation
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  first=[1000,2000,3000,_,_,_] (m=3)   second=[2500,2600,5000] (n=3)
  i=2 j=2 k=5
    │
    ▼
  while j>=0: place max(first[i], second[j]) at k, move that ptr and k back
    │ 3000 vs 5000 → k5=5000  j=1
    │ 3000 vs 2600 → k4=3000  i=1
    │ 2000 vs 2600 → k3=2600  j=0
    │ 2000 vs 2500 → k2=2500  j=-1  (second done)
    ▼
  first=[1000,2000,2500,2600,3000,5000]  (1000,2000 already placed)
    ▼
  Output: in-place sorted merged ledger
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging two sorted arrays in-place takes a first array with spare capacity at its end and a second sorted array and merges the second into the first so the whole thing stays sorted, without allocating a separate output array. I do it in linear time and constant space by writing from the back: three pointers start at the last real element of each input and the very last slot of the first array, and I copy the larger of the two compared tails into the write position, moving backward.

Writing from the back rather than the front is the entire trick. Merging from the front would overwrite elements of the first array that have not been merged yet, but the back of the first array is exactly its free capacity, so writing there never clobbers a value I still need. I keep the invariant that the write pointer is always at or ahead of the read pointer in the first array, which guarantees safety.

The subtle correctness point is when to stop. I stop as soon as the second array is exhausted, not when both are, because any elements left in the first array are already sitting in their correct positions and were never moved, whereas leftover elements of the second array would still need to be placed at the front. Getting that asymmetry right is what separates a correct implementation from a common buggy one. For money I compare with BigDecimal so amounts are exact, and I handle an empty second array as a no-op.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to consolidate Priya's shared transactions into Rajesh's pre-sized ledger array so a statement generator could read one sorted list, with no second allocation even for large ledgers. Explaining the write-from-the-back reasoning, the pointer invariant, and the stop-when-second-exhausted rule shows the interviewer that I understand why the in-place merge is structured the way it is.
